records.place: San Casciano in Val di Pesa, Chianti Classico zone, Tuscany

wine.name: Tignanello
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, the category Italian law created in 1992
wine.grapes: Sangiovese, about four fifths, with Cabernet Sauvignon and a little Cabernet Franc, the blend the house has kept since the 1982 vintage.
wine.sites: The Tignanello vineyard alone, on the family's estate of that name between the Greve and Pesa valleys: slopes facing south west at about 350 to 400 metres, on stony, limestone rich soils of Pliocene marine marl with alberese, on the same hillside as Solaia.
wine.making: The berries are destemmed and sorted by hand, then fermented and macerated on their skins in tanks for one to three weeks, and the malolactic conversion is finished in barrel. The wine spends about twelve to eighteen months in small barrels, French oak with a little Hungarian, the lots blended a few months before bottling, and about a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, red plum and iris drawn tight by cassis and cedar, with tobacco leaf and a touch of vanilla from the barrique; medium to full bodied, with fresh Sangiovese acidity and fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Approachable five or six years after the vintage, it is at its fullest between about ten and twenty years and keeps longer in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The vineyard on the family's estate in the Chianti Classico zone that gives every grape in the wine.
The regional category for Tuscany; the first vintages, made before the category existed, were sold as Vino da Tavola.
The Florentine family house, in the wine trade since 1385 by its own account.

records.table: Tignanello is Marchesi Antinori's Sangiovese with Cabernet from one vineyard in the Chianti Classico zone, first sold outside the Chianti rules with the 1971 vintage and aged in small French barrels. Cherry and iris meet cassis and cedar over firm tannin; decant it young.
records.story: By the family's own account, a forebear joined the Florentine guild of wine merchants, the Arte dei Vinattieri, in 1385, and in 1506 a descendant bought the palace in Florence that bears the family name. For centuries the house traded wine and made Chianti. The modern turn came from the Tignanello vineyard, with the house oenologist Giacomo Tachis (1933 to 2016). The 1970 was made there as a Chianti Classico Riserva, with Canaiolo and a little white Trebbiano and Malvasia as the rules then required, and aged in small oak barrels. With the 1971 vintage the family left the Chianti rules and sold the wine as a Vino da Tavola della Toscana, named for its vineyard. With the 1975 vintage the white grapes were gone, and by the 1982 vintage the blend had settled at about four fifths Sangiovese with Cabernet Sauvignon and a little Cabernet Franc. By the house's account it was the first Sangiovese raised in small barrels and among the first Chianti Classico reds made without white grapes. Solaia, its Cabernet led sibling from the same hillside, followed in 1978, and when Italian law created the IGT category in 1992, such wines found a legal home. Learn it as a founding Super Tuscan: the 1971 date, and Sangiovese in the lead.

others.name: Solaia
others.note: The Cabernet Sauvignon led sibling from the same hillside, first made in 1978, with Sangiovese added in later vintages.

others.name: Badia a Passignano
others.note: Chianti Classico Gran Selezione from the family's Badia a Passignano estate: Sangiovese inside the appellation.

others.name: Guado al Tasso
others.note: The family's estate in Bolgheri and its Bolgheri Superiore, a blend of Bordeaux grapes.

traps: Tignanello is Sangiovese led with Cabernet; Solaia is Cabernet Sauvignon led with Sangiovese. Reversing them is the usual error.
Tignanello is made only in years the family judges fit: there is none of 1972, 1973, 1974, 1976, 1984, 1992 or 2002.
The IGT category did not exist in 1971, so the early vintages were labelled Vino da Tavola.

cards.front: Tignanello: what changed between the 1970 and the 1971 vintage?
cards.back: The 1970 was a Chianti Classico Riserva with white grapes; the 1971 left the Chianti rules and was sold as Vino da Tavola under the vineyard's name.

cards.front: Which Antinori red is Cabernet Sauvignon led, from the hillside it shares with Tignanello?

opts: Sangiovese with Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc
Cabernet Sauvignon with Sangiovese and Cabernet Franc
Sangiovese with Canaiolo, Trebbiano and Malvasia
Sangiovese alone from the Tignanello vineyard
questions.exp: Since 1982 Tignanello has been about four fifths Sangiovese with Cabernet Sauvignon and a little Cabernet Franc; the Cabernet led blend is Solaia's, and the white grapes left in 1975.

questions.q: With which vintage did Antinori first sell Tignanello outside the Chianti rules, as a table wine named for its vineyard?
questions.exp: The 1971 was sold as Vino da Tavola della Toscana; the 1970 had been a Chianti Classico Riserva, 1975 dropped the white grapes and 1978 is Solaia's first vintage.

report: The vintages, blends, site and making rest on Antinori's own pages (historical data, soil, vinification sheets of 2009 to 2023, the family page and the Solaia historical data), read through search summaries; the vintage sheets give twelve to eighteen months in barrel and one to three weeks of maceration, so the making gives ranges.

Cabernet's year of arrival is left out: Gambero Rosso gives 1975, one retailer the 1971, and Antinori's own historical data and Wikipedia date only the end of the white grapes to 1975 and the settled blend to 1982, which the story follows. The house's claims to the first Sangiovese in barrique and the first modern red with Cabernet stand hedged as its own account, the Cabernet one softened to among the first Tuscan reds; several secondary accounts in the search repeat the barrique claim.

Giacomo Tachis (1933 to 2016) is dated by Decanter's news of his death at 82 in February 2016 and by Wikipedia and Meininger for the birth year of 1933; the forebear of 1385 and the buyer of the palace in 1506 are described, since their dates were not found.
The Bordeaux oenologist who advised the house in the early 1970s is left out: one account only. The commercial release of the 1971 in 1974 rests on one source and is left out.
The library's w-tignanello sets the vineyard at the Santa Cristina estate; Antinori's own pages name the estate Tenuta Tignanello in the Mercatale Val di Pesa zone, which the record follows.
The library's p-marchesi-antinori says IGT Toscana was created in 1992; the category IGT came with the law of 1992, which the record says, without dating IGT Toscana itself.
Search count for this record: 8 of the group's 33 (Antinori's domain six times, two open searches); the vintages not made rest on Antinori's historical data and Wikipedia.

changed: place: was Mercatale Val di Pesa; now San Casciano in Val di Pesa, the commune every address listing for the Tignanello estate gives, since Mercatale is one of its hamlets and no page read tied the estate to it by name.
wine.sites: was near Mercatale Val di Pesa, on marine marl; now between the Greve and Pesa valleys, on Pliocene marine marl with alberese, as the house's estate and product pages put it.

wine.making: was mostly new French oak with a little Hungarian; now French oak with a little Hungarian, since the house's sheets give French oak with a smaller share of Hungarian and no share of new barrels.

story: was among the first modern Tuscan reds to use Cabernet, under the house's name; now among the first Chianti Classico reds made without white grapes, the house's own words, since its Cabernet claim is a bare first (the first modern red blended with Cabernet) that the record should neither soften under its name nor repeat.
story: was Here the Super Tuscan begins; now Learn it as a founding Super Tuscan, since no source read makes Tignanello the first of the category.
open: The maceration of one to three weeks rests on the house's vintage sheets (15 to 20 days in the 2010 sheet); the destemming and hand sorting are confirmed for the 2009 and 2011 sheets only.

The library's w-tignanello places the vineyard at the Santa Cristina estate; a page drawn from Wikipedia calls the Tignanello vineyard part of the Santa Cristina estate, also known as Tenuta Tignanello, so the author's tension is not upheld and is left to the integrator.
The glass and the ageing rest on the author's sources and the library; no tasting note of the house's own was read by the refuter.

records.place: Brolio, Gaiole in Chianti, Chianti Classico, Tuscany

wine.name: Castello di Brolio
wine.classification: Gran Selezione, the tier of Chianti Classico above Riserva, approved in 2013
wine.grapes: Sangiovese, the great majority, at times with a little of another red grape; the rules for Gran Selezione have since asked for nine tenths Sangiovese or more.
wine.sites: Vineyards around the castle at Brolio, up to about 490 metres in the house's sheets, on the three soils of Chianti Classico: macigno sandstone, galestro of the Scaglia Toscana and alberese limestone of the Monte Morello formation.
wine.making: Fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel at about 24 to 27 degrees Celsius, with some two weeks on the skins. The wine then spends eighteen months to almost two years in 500 litre tonneaux, about a third of them new, and a few months in bottle before release. The first vintage, the 1997, was raised in barriques.
wine.glass: Red cherry, violet and iris with dried herbs, liquorice and a touch of cedar from the tonneaux; firm, fine grained tannin and bright acidity carry it to a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it opens from about six to eight years after the vintage and keeps for fifteen to twenty years in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a large, wide bowled glass.

label.means: The DOCG of the historic Chianti zone between Florence and Siena, its bounds first drawn by a Grand Ducal edict of 1716.
The category above Riserva: grapes from the bottler's own vineyards and at least thirty months of ageing, three of them in bottle.
One of the eleven village units the rules allow on Gran Selezione alone, printed on this wine from the 2020 vintage.
The black rooster of the consorzio, on every bottle of Chianti Classico since 2005.

records.table: Castello di Brolio is Barone Ricasoli's Chianti Classico Gran Selezione, Sangiovese from the vineyards around Brolio, the castle at Gaiole the family has held since 1141 by its own account. Red cherry and iris over firm, fine tannin; give it an hour in a decanter.
records.story: A document in the family archive shows the Ricasoli holding the castle of Brolio in 1141, and the house has made wine there for centuries. Bettino Ricasoli (1809 to 1880), the Iron Baron, twice prime minister of the new Kingdom of Italy, set down his view of Chianti in 1872, in a letter to a professor at the University of Pisa: a wine led by Sangiovese, with Canaiolo to soften it and the white Malvasia. Blends of that kind shaped Chianti's rules for a century. Around 1970 the family sold the Brolio name to the drinks group Seagram while keeping the land, and the brand later passed to the Australian house of Hardy's. In 1993 the family bought back the brand and the winery and set about replanting the vineyards; Castello di Brolio, the estate's new flagship, followed with the 1997 vintage, which by the house's account made its name abroad. When the consorzio's members approved Gran Selezione in 2013, the wine took its place in the new tier, and from the 2020 vintage its label adds the village unit Gaiole. Know Bettino and his three grapes for the examination, and pour this wine as the castle's own answer, from the soils around it.

others.name: Colledilà
others.note: Chianti Classico Gran Selezione from a single vineyard of the Brolio estate.

others.name: Brolio Chianti Classico

others.name: Casalferro
others.note: The estate's Merlot, sold outside the Chianti Classico DOCG.

traps: Bettino Ricasoli's Chianti of 1872 included the white Malvasia; white grapes have been forbidden in Chianti Classico since 2006.
Brolio and Castello di Brolio are two wines: the first is the estate's Chianti Classico, the second its Gran Selezione from the vineyards around the castle.
Gran Selezione asks for estate grapes and long ageing; it does not ask for a single vineyard.

cards.back: A professor at the University of Pisa; Sangiovese led, with Canaiolo and the white Malvasia.

cards.front: Castello di Brolio: on which three soils do its vineyards around the castle lie?

A single vineyard named on the label

questions.q: In which year did the Ricasoli family buy back the Brolio brand and winery from the drinks trade?
questions.exp: The family regained the brand and the winery in 1993, after the Seagram and Hardy's years; 1872 is Bettino Ricasoli's letter, 1984 Chianti's DOCG and 2013 the vote for Gran Selezione.

report: The castle in 1141, the letter of 1872 and the 1997 vintage that made the estate's name rest on Ricasoli's own pages; the sites, making and blends on its product sheets of 2011, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2021 and 2022 (2015 with Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot, 2016 with Abrusco, 2021 Sangiovese alone); the Gran Selezione rules, the eleven village units, the edict of 1716, the rooster of 2005 and the vote of 2013 on the consorzio's pages.

Bettino Ricasoli's dates and his two terms as prime minister rest on two secondary pages of the same search (Eat Magazine and The Wine Collective); the professor of 1872 is described, his dates not found.

The sale to Seagram is dated to the 1960s by Decanter and to the start of the 1970s by two others, so the story says around 1970; the passage to Hardy's and the return of 1993 rest on two secondary accounts each, whose pages the search summary did not tell apart beyond Wein-Plus and Montecristo Magazine.
The first vintage of Castello di Brolio was not found; the house shows a 1997 as Gran Selezione on its own site, though the category was approved only in 2013, so the record gives no first year.

Wikipedia notes that Ricasoli's letters do not bear out the exact proportions later credited to him, so no proportion is given; the library's p-barone-ricasoli calls it a formula, which the record softens to his view.
The library's Colledila lacks the accent the house prints (Colledilà); the library's holdings line calls Brolio the largest single property in Chianti Classico, a size claim the record leaves out.
Search count for this record: 6 of the group's 33, with two more shared by the group on the consorzio's rules and history.

changed: wine.classification: was Gran Selezione with the 2021 and 2022 adding Gaiole; now Gran Selezione, the tier of Chianti Classico above Riserva, approved in 2013, since a list of recent vintages is volatile and the village unit is taught on the label.

wine.grapes: was a vintage by vintage list (the 2021 alone, the 2015 with Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot, the 2016 with Abrusco); now the typical blend, Sangiovese with at times a little of another red grape, and the nine tenths rule the consorzio's production code gives for Gran Selezione.

wine.sites: was six vineyards at about 400 to 490 metres; now the vineyards around the castle, up to about 490 metres in the house's sheets, since no page read counts six and the house's 2011 sheet gives 250 to 450 metres.
wine.making: the first vintage, the 1997, raised in barriques, added from the house's 1997 sheet (eighteen months in barriques).
wine.label: Gaiole was printed on the 2021 and 2022 vintages; now on this wine from the 2020 vintage, since the house's own page for the 2020 already carries Gaiole and the 2019 does not.
table: six vineyards cut, and the castle held since 1141 is now said by the family's own account.

story: the first vintage of 1997 restored, Castello di Brolio the estate's new flagship, on the house's 1997 sheet and a merchant's page; the replanting no longer said to span the decade before it; the 2021 as Sangiovese alone replaced by the village unit Gaiole from the 2020 vintage.
others: the village unit year of Colledilà and the Colorino of the 2021 Brolio cut as vintage reports; Brolio is now the Chianti Classico released younger than the Gran Selezione.
cards: the second card no longer counts six vineyards.
open: The sale to Seagram is dated to the 1960s in one account and to the early 1970s in another, so around 1970 stands; one account has Seagram selling to United Wine Producers before Hardy's, and the record names only Hardy's.

Whether Bettino Ricasoli kept Malvasia for wines drunk young and out of wines for ageing was searched and not confirmed; the record keeps the three grapes as his view, and the 70, 15, 15 split is left out as disputed.
The share of new tonneaux, a third, rests on the house's 2019 and 2022 sheets (30 per cent); earlier sheets were not read for it.

records.place: Panzano, Greve in Chianti, Chianti Classico zone, Tuscany

wine.name: Flaccianello della Pieve
wine.grapes: Sangiovese alone, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: At first the Flaccianello vineyard alone; from early in the 2000s a selection of the estate's own parcels in the Conca d'Oro, the amphitheatre of slopes below Panzano, on calcareous clay and schist at height.
wine.making: Wild yeasts ferment the grapes in stainless steel, with at least three weeks on the skins. The wine then spends eighteen months to two years in French oak, mostly barriques of Allier and Tronçais, and later vintages finish in larger casks before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and iris with espresso, liquorice and warm earth; full and ripe for Sangiovese, held in line by firm, polished tannin and fresh acidity to a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and closed in youth, it opens from about eight years after the vintage and keeps for twenty years or more in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for one to two hours, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The wine's name, first given to one vineyard's Sangiovese and kept for the estate's selection.
The regional category of the hills of central Tuscany, chosen in place of Chianti Classico though the estate lies inside the zone.
The estate in the Conca d'Oro below Panzano, bought in 1968 by a family of terracotta makers.

records.table: Flaccianello della Pieve is Fontodi's Sangiovese alone from the Conca d'Oro below Panzano, first made in 1981 and sold as an IGT though it grows inside the Chianti Classico zone. Dark cherry, iris and espresso over polished tannin; decant it and give it a large glass.
records.story: In 1968 a family long known in Chianti for its terracotta tiles bought Fontodi, a farm in the valley below Panzano called the Conca d'Oro, the golden shell, for its amphitheatre shape as the estate tells it. With the 1981 vintage the family made a wine of Sangiovese alone, from a vineyard called Flaccianello. The Chianti rules of the day required white grapes in the blend, so the wine stood outside the appellation; it has stayed outside, labelled Colli della Toscana Centrale IGT, although the rules have since changed and Sangiovese alone may be Chianti Classico. Through the 1980s and 1990s the wine was the vineyard's own; early in the 2000s it became a selection of the estate's parcels in the Conca d'Oro, while Vigna del Sorbo stayed inside the appellation as the estate's single vineyard Chianti Classico. The estate is farmed organically and certified, and it fires terracotta of its own. With Le Pergole Torte, first made in 1977, and Cepparello, first made in 1980, Flaccianello shows a second line of the Super Tuscan story, one with no Cabernet in it at all. Learn it as the riper, darker voice of Panzano Sangiovese.

Flaccianello is labelled Colli della Toscana Centrale IGT, not Toscana IGT and not Chianti Classico.
Panzano is a village of Greve in Chianti and one of the village units of Chianti Classico, not a commune of its own.

report: The purchase of 1968, the terracotta, the organic certificate, the Conca d'Oro and its soils rest on Fontodi's own pages read through search; the Flaccianello page itself did not reach the search tool and one WebFetch of fontodi.com was refused by the network and not retried.

The first vintage of 1981 and the Colli della Toscana Centrale IGT rest on Decanter, Jancis Robinson's tasting notes and retailers' sheets; the single vineyard until about 2000 and the selection after it on Decanter (2001) and Best of Wines (until 2000), so the record says about 2000.

The making (wild yeasts, steel, three weeks and more on the skins, about two years in Allier and Tronçais barriques) rests on several retailers' sheets agreeing with Decanter; Decanter's account of the barrel time rising from twelve to twenty four months, the share of new oak and a recent final spell in larger casks rests on it alone and is left out.

The library's w-flaccianello gives its category as Toscana IGT; the label, Decanter and Jancis Robinson give Colli della Toscana Centrale IGT, which the record follows, and the region's producers line calls it a Toscana IGT too.

Left out for want of a second source: della Pieve as a nod to the Romanesque Pieve di San Leolino above Panzano (one retailer), the 1981 meant as a single vintage, and the highest parcels at 480 metres on pietraforte.
founded is left empty: the house's own pages date the family's purchase, not a founding, and the farm is older. The family's founder of 1968 is described, not named.
Search count for this record: 6 of the group's 33 and one refused WebFetch.

changed: wine.sites: was since about 2000; now from early in the 2000s, since Decanter and a merchant's note date the first selection to the 2001 vintage and Wine Watch keeps the single vineyard until the 2004 vintage.

wine.making: was temperature controlled steel, malolactic in barrel, about two years in Allier and Tronçais barriques; now steel, at least three weeks on the skins, eighteen months to two years in French oak, mostly those barriques, with later vintages finishing in larger casks, since merchants give 24 months in barriques and French oak barrels for the 2021, a critic 18 months for the 2014 and Decanter a last spell in 25 hectolitre casks; the temperature control and the malolactic in barrel were found in no source read.
wine.label: Fontodi was in one family's hands since 1968; now bought in 1968 by a family of terracotta makers, so that ownership is told as history.
story: roof tiles is now terracotta tiles, the word of the house's own page; the Conca d'Oro is named for its amphitheatre shape as the estate tells it; to this day is now has stayed outside.

story: was the family kept Vigna del Sorbo for its Chianti Classico Gran Selezione around 2000; now Vigna del Sorbo stayed inside the appellation as the estate's single vineyard Chianti Classico, since Gran Selezione was approved only in 2013.
cards: the Conca d'Oro card was for its amphitheatre shape alone; now Fontodi's account beside the wheat that travel accounts give for the gold.
open: The first vintage is 1981 in Decanter and most accounts, 1980 in one merchant's; the record follows 1981 with the library.
Wine Watch describes the old single vineyard as surrounding the parish church of Panzano, a second account for della Pieve; the church's name was not confirmed, so the name stays unexplained.
The soils (calcareous clay and schist) and the heights rest on the author's reading of the house's pages and were not retested.

records.place: Radda in Chianti, Chianti Classico zone, Tuscany

wine.name: Le Pergole Torte
wine.sites: The estate's historic vineyards above Radda, planted between 1968 and 1999, among them the Le Pergole Torte vineyard of 1968, which faces north north east; the house stands at about 425 metres.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented with two pump overs a day in glass lined cement vats, with no temperature control, for about three weeks; the malolactic conversion also takes place in cement. The wine then spends about twelve months in Allier barriques and twelve in casks of Slavonian oak, and some three months in bottle.
wine.glass: Pale ruby; sour cherry, rosehip and violet with dried herbs and a cold, stony edge; light on its feet, with high acidity, fine, taut tannin and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first years, it opens from about eight to ten years after the vintage and lasts for decades in a strong year.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass for its perfume.

label.means: The name of a vineyard of the estate, planted in 1968, given to the wine since its first vintage of 1977.
The regional category for Tuscany; the estate bottles nothing as Chianti Classico, by its own choice.
The estate above Radda, bought in 1967, and also the name of its Sangiovese blend with Canaiolo and Colorino.

records.table: Le Pergole Torte is Montevertine's Sangiovese alone from high vineyards above Radda, first made in 1977 and sold outside Chianti Classico since the estate left the consorzio in 1981. Pale and perfumed, rosehip and sour cherry over taut tannin; pour it in a wide glass.
records.story: In 1967 a steel industrialist bought Montevertine, a farmhouse above Radda, as a place for holidays. He restored the house, planted vines, set up a small cellar to make wine for friends and clients, and sold his first vintage, the 1971, as Chianti Classico Montevertine. With the 1977 vintage he made a wine of Sangiovese alone and named it for his Le Pergole Torte vineyard, by the estate's account the first of its kind in the Radda zone. The Chianti rules of the day required white Trebbiano and Malvasia in the blend; he refused to add them, and in 1981 he left the Chianti Classico consorzio. From 1982 his wines carried no Chianti name at all, and Le Pergole Torte was sold as table wine and later as Toscana IGT. In the 1980s its label took a woman's face drawn by an artist friend of the founder, in designs that vary from vintage to vintage. The vineyards have been farmed organically since 2009. The rules moved towards him, white grapes leaving Chianti Classico in 2006 and Sangiovese alone becoming lawful, but the estate has stayed outside. The lesson for a sommelier: an estate that left its appellation to be purer, not more international.

others.name: Montevertine
others.note: The estate's red of Sangiovese with a little Canaiolo and Colorino, sold as Chianti Classico Montevertine from 1971 to 1981.

others.name: Pian del Ciampolo

report: The purchase of 1967, the first vintage of 1971, the Chianti Classico Montevertine of 1971 to 1981 and the exit from the consorzio before 1982, the first Pergole Torte of 1977, the vineyards, the cement and the two years in wood, and organic farming since 2009 rest on the estate's own pages read through search.

The year of the exit, 1981, and the white grapes as its cause rest on the house's 1982 with two secondary accounts (Skurnik and Primal Wine); the label's woman's face by an artist friend on We Wealth and Mad Rose, whose dates for it differ (1982, or all bottles only from 1988), so the story says the 1980s.

The founder is described, not named with dates: one source only gives his death in November 2000 and none his birth; the artist is described for the same reason. Giulio Gambelli, named in one account as the founder's friend, is left out.

The library's w-le-pergole-torte calls it the first single vineyard Sangiovese of the modern era and a single high vineyard; the house claims only the first pure Sangiovese of the Radda zone and draws the wine from historic vineyards planted between 1968 and 1999, which the record follows.
The library's p-montevertine names the founder's son, a living man; the record does not.
The estate's sheets give twenty or twenty five days of fermentation; the record says about three weeks.

open: Wine Spectator's obituary of the founder gives 1968 for the purchase; the house's own page and the trade give 1967, which stands with the library.

One account dates the exit from the consorzio to 1982; the house sells Chianti Classico Montevertine from 1971 to 1981 and plain Montevertine from 1982 after the exit, and 1981 stands on two secondary accounts.

The founder died in 2000 by Wine Spectator's obituary, his birth year not found, so he stays described; the artist of the labels is named in one account only, dating the series from 1982, and stays described.

wine.name: Cepparello
wine.sites: A selection of grapes from the estate's older vineyards in the western hills of the Chianti Classico zone, at about 350 to 450 metres, mostly on galestro, a rocky schist and clay.
wine.making: The grapes macerate on their skins for longer than those of the estate's Chianti Classico. The wine is then raised for eighteen months or more in small French oak barrels, about a third of them new, and rests in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Red cherry, violet and dried herbs with orange peel and a touch of cedar; medium bodied and fresh, with fine, chalky tannin, drawn long rather than broad.
wine.ageing: Fragrant within a few years of the vintage, it is at its fullest from about eight to fifteen years and keeps longer in a strong year.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a large, wide bowled glass.

label.means: A name the estate chose for the wine, not a village and not a vineyard designation.
The regional category for Tuscany, which the wine carries because it was born outside the Chianti rules.
The estate named for two neighbouring hamlets, Isole and Olena, bought and joined as one in 1956.

records.table: Cepparello is Isole e Olena's Sangiovese alone, first made in 1980 from the estate's old vines in the western hills of Chianti Classico; it spends a year and a half or more in French barriques. Red cherry, violet and dried herbs, drawn fine and long; decant it for an hour.
records.story: In 1956 a family from Piedmont bought two neighbouring estates at San Donato in Poggio, around the hamlets of Isole and Olena, and joined them as one. The founder's son took charge in the middle of the 1970s and set out to learn what Sangiovese could do on its own. The view in Chianti then held that a fine wine could not be made from Sangiovese alone, and the rules required white grapes in the blend. In 1980 he bottled the first Cepparello, pure Sangiovese from the estate's old vines, sold outside the appellation as a table wine; it later took the Toscana IGT label. By the accounts read, its name comes from a small stream, the Borro Cepparello, that runs among the estate's vineyards. With Le Pergole Torte and Flaccianello it became one of the Sangiovese wines that left Chianti Classico to be purer rather than more international. The estate also grew known for its Vin Santo, and for small plantings of Syrah, Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon. In 2022, after more than six decades in one family, Isole e Olena was sold to the EPI group. Pour Cepparello as the western hills' answer to Panzano and Radda: perfume and clarity rather than weight.

report: The first vintage of 1980, Sangiovese alone, the Toscana IGT and the break with the view that Sangiovese could not stand alone rest on the estate's own shop pages; its history page did not reach the search tool.

The purchase of 1956 and the joining of the two estates rest on Decanter and Italy's Finest Wines; the son's charge from the late 1970s on two secondary accounts; the sale to the EPI group in 2022 on Italy's Finest Wines and Vinatis. The founder and his son are described, not named: the son is living, the father's dates were not found.

The making rests on Liberty Wines and Click Wine (eighteen months, a third new) and The World of Fine Wine (a longer maceration than the Chianti Classico); the sites on Liberty Wines and Folio Wine (galestro, 350 to 450 metres, the oldest vineyards). The World of Fine Wine's first vintage raised in chestnut casks rests on it alone and is left out.

The stream, the Borro Cepparello, rests on two search summaries whose pages were not told apart (Liberty Wines or Folio, Italy's Finest Wines or Winestar), so the story hedges it and the label line does not repeat it.

The library's p-isole-e-olena and w-cepparello name the founder's son, a living man; the record does not. The library's Collezione De Marchi Syrah is left out of others for the same reason, and the wine is now sold as Collezione Privata by one importer.
founded is left empty: 1956 is the family's purchase of two older properties, one account calls it the founding of the modern estate, and the library gives no year.
